lines: נַקְרִיב לוֹ שֶׁבַח נָאֶה — שִׁיר הָאַהֲבָה

review: The hymn is a narrative of redemption: 2:2 is 1 Cor 15:3 with Phil 2:8 (מֵת … בְּמִשְׁמַעַת), 2:4 is Heb 7:25 (מֵלִיץ) with Mark 16:19, 3:3–5 is Ps 23:1 with Eph 1:7, and 4:3–4 is 1 Thess 4:16–17. The Arabic عَشَاء / رِوَايَة is 'tale, narrative', which Hebrew renders with סִפּוּר rather than a modern story-word.
1:1–2 is the printed two-line call to sing, with the triple زَنِّمُوا kept as a triple imperative זַמְּרוּ; the Hebrew does not reduce it to one, since the repetition is the tune's whole opening.

2:1 and 3:1 and 4:1 all begin סִפּוּר אַהֲבַת … but with a different third element (הַנִּפְלָא, הַנֶּאֱמָן, פּוֹדֵה הַפּוֹשְׁעִים), exactly as the Arabic varies الْعَجِيب / الْأَمِين / فَادِي الْخُطَاه; the variation is the stanza's structure and is preserved.

3:2 שְׁנֵה — the Arabic أَعِدْهَا is 'repeat it'; the Hebrew uses the imperative of שָׁנָה (Deut 17:18, מִשְׁנֵה הַתּוֹרָה), the verb behind the whole practice of reciting a text again, so the line asks for rehearsal and not merely for a second telling.

4:2 מִלֵּא לִבִּי תַּאֲוָה לִרְאוֹתוֹ — the Arabic قَدْ مَلأتْ قَلْبِي شَوْقًا لِأَنْ أَرَاه is 'filled my heart with longing to see Him'; תַּאֲוָה is the biblical noun for desire (Ps 10:3, 21:3) and is kept in the construct, so the longing is the object that fills the heart rather than a vague emotion.
